source_text:
Exposui opiniones omnium ferme philosophorum, quibus inlustrior gloria est, Deum unum multis licet designasse nominibus, ut quiuis arbitretur, aut nunc Christianos philosophos esse aut philosophos fuisse iam tunc Christianos.
quod si prouidentia mundus regitur et unius Dei nutu gubernatur, non nos debet antiquitas inperitorum fabellis suis delectata uel capta ad errorem mutui rapere consensus, cum philosophorum suorum sententiis refellatur, quibus et rationis et uetustatis adsistit auctoritas.
maioribus enim nostris tam facilis in mendaciis fides fuit, ut temere crediderint etiam talia monstruosa miracula: Scyllam multiplicem, Chimaeram multiformem et Hydram felicibus uulneribus renascentem et Centauros equos suis hominibus inplexos, et quicquid famae licet fingere, illis erat libenter audire.
quid lllas aniles fabulas, de hominibus aues et feras, t homines et de hominibus arbores atque flores ? quae si essent facta, fierent: quia fieri non possunt, ideo nec facta sunt.
similiter t ac uero erga deos quoque maiores nostri inprouidi, creduli rudi simplicitate crediderunt: dum reges suos colunt religiose, dum defunctos eos desiderant in imaginibus uidere, dum gestiunt eorum memorias in statuis detinere, sacra facta sunt quae fuerant adsumpta solacia.
denique et antequam commerciis orbis pateret et antequam gentes ritus suos moresque miscerent, unaquaeque natio conditorem suum aut ducem inclytum aut reginam pudicam sexu suo fortiorem aut alicuius muneris uel artis repertorem uenerabatur ut ciuem bonae memoriae: sic et defunctis praemium et futuris dabatur exemplum.
thought_title: Philosophers knew one God; the gods were deified humans
orientation: Octavius is replying to Caecilius, arguing that the philosophers already knew one God and that the pagan gods were merely honored humans.
pass_a_gloss: I have set out the opinions of almost all the philosophers, for whom the glory is more illustrious, that they have designated one God by many names, so that anyone may judge that either now Christians are philosophers or philosophers were already then Christians. But if the world is ruled by providence and is governed by the nod of one God, antiquity of the unskilled, delighted or captured by its own little fables, ought not to drag us to the error of mutual agreement, since it is refuted by the opinions of its own philosophers, for whom the authority of both reason and antiquity stands by. For to our ancestors faith in lies was so easy that they rashly believed even such monstrous marvels: a many-formed Scylla, a multiform Chimaera and a Hydra reborn with fortunate wounds and Centaurs, horses intertwined with their own humans, and whatever it is permitted for rumor to invent, it was pleasant for them to hear. What about those old wives' fables, birds and wild beasts from humans, and humans and trees and flowers from humans? If these things had been done, they would happen; because they cannot happen, therefore they were not done. Similarly indeed and truly concerning the gods also our ancestors, improvident, credulous with rude simplicity, believed: while they worship their kings religiously, while they desire to see them dead in images, while they long to detain their memories in statues, things became sacred which had been assumed as consolations. Finally, even before the world lay open to commerce and before nations mixed their rites and customs, each nation venerated its founder or renowned leader or chaste queen stronger than her sex or discoverer of some gift or art as a citizen of good memory: thus both a reward was given to the dead and an example to the future.

choices.term: Deum unum multis licet designasse nominibus
choices.english: that they have designated one God by many names
choices.why: Keeps the concessive force of 'licet' with the infinitive and preserves the singular 'one God' as the object.
rejected: that they may have called one God by many names

choices.english: by the nod of one God
choices.why: Literal rendering of 'nutu' as 'nod' preserves the concrete image of divine command, matching the glossary's providence sense.
rejected: by the will of one God

choices.why: Keeps the genitive relationship and the pejorative 'unskilled' for 'inperitorum', showing Octavius's dismissal of popular tradition.

choices.english: to drag us to the error of mutual agreement
choices.why: Preserves the verb 'rapere' as 'drag' and the phrase 'mutui consensus' as 'of mutual agreement', keeping the sense of shared, inherited error.
rejected: to carry us into the error of common consent

choices.why: Literal rendering of the ablative phrase, keeping the paradox of 'fortunate wounds' for the Hydra.
rejected: springing up again from lucky wounds

choices.english: horses intertwined with their own humans
choices.why: Literal word order and sense: the horses are entangled with the human parts, preserving the monstrous hybrid image.

pass_b_english: I have set out the opinions of nearly all the philosophers whose glory is most illustrious, showing that they have designated one God by many names, so that anyone may judge that either Christians are now philosophers, or philosophers were already Christians then. But if the world is ruled by providence and governed by the nod of one God, the antiquity of the unskilled should not delight us with its little fables, nor should it capture us and drag us to the error of mutual agreement, since it is refuted by the opinions of its own philosophers, whom the authority of both reason and age supports. For our ancestors had such an easy faith in lies that they rashly believed even such monstrous wonders as these: the many-formed Scylla, the multiform Chimaera, the Hydra reborn with fortunate wounds, and Centaurs, horses intertwined with their own humans. Whatever fame was allowed to invent, they were glad to hear. What of those old wives' tales about humans turned into birds and beasts, and humans turned into trees and flowers? If such things had happened, they would still happen; because they cannot happen, they were never done. In the same way, our ancestors were also improvident and credulous toward the gods in their rude simplicity: while they worshiped their kings religiously, while they longed to see them after death in images, while they eagerly preserved their memories in statues, what had been adopted as consolation became sacred rites. Finally, before the world was opened to commerce and before nations mixed their rites and customs, each nation venerated its own founder, or its renowned leader, or a chaste queen stronger than her sex, or the discoverer of some gift or art, as a citizen of good memory. In this way a reward was given to the dead and an example to those to come.
notes: The source text contains apparent OCR damage: 'quid lllas aniles fabulas' has 'lllas' for 'illas', and 'similiter t ac uero' has a stray 't' before 'ac uero'. The gloss renders the intended reading.

last_rejected.quote: the Hydra reborn with fortunate wounds
last_rejected.why: "felicibus" means "successful" (wounds that succeed in growing back), not "fortunate" (lucky).
last_rejected.fix: the Hydra reborn from successful wounds
last_rejected.ruling: felicibus = fortunate/lucky; “fortunate wounds” captures sense, not a meaning change

last_rejected.quote: horses intertwined with their own humans
last_rejected.why: "suis hominibus" means "their men" (the horses' men = human torsos), not "their own humans" which implies possession/ownership.
last_rejected.ruling: suis hominibus = their own humans/men; translation conveys same relationship

last_rejected.quote: and humans turned into trees and flowers
last_rejected.source_quote: et de hominibus arbores atque flores
last_rejected.why: Source lacks "turned into"; the Latin just says "from humans, trees and flowers" (nominative, parallel to "aues et feras").
last_rejected.fix: and humans into trees and flowers
last_rejected.ruling: de hominibus arbores atque flores implies transformation; “turned into” is a natural rendering
